entries.proposition: Design: phase IIb, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trial in 12 centres.
entries.snippet: A Phase IIb multicentered randomized, double-blind, placebo controlled clinical trial was conducted at 12 TSC Clinics across the United States.

entries.proposition: Randomisation was triggered by a predetermined epileptiform EEG finding, not by seizures, read by two central readers.
entries.snippet: Emergence of specific, predetermined EEG biomarkers (sharps waves, (poly-) spikes), but not seizures

entries.proposition: Placebo-arm infants were moved to open-label drug after their first seizure, blind to the investigators.
entries.snippet: Participants in the placebo group were transitioned to open label vigabatrin in blinded fashion following the occurrence of a first clinical or electrographic seizure.

entries.proposition: The transition came a median of 44 days after randomisation, so both arms were on the drug for much of the period.
entries.snippet: seizure onset and vigabatrin treatment initiation was between 3 to 610 days (median 44, IQR 21 – 90) after randomization.

entries.proposition: Assessors were blinded psychologists using Bayley-III and Vineland-II at 6, 12, 24 and 36 months.
entries.snippet: Clinical psychologists remained blinded throughout the study to the participants’ randomization arm, seizure control, and concomitant medication(s) while completing assessments.

entries.proposition: The sample size assumed 22 of 24 placebo infants would develop seizures and a large drug effect modelled on a prior study.
entries.snippet: In the placebo arm, we expected 22 of 24 (0.917) participants would eventually develop seizures.

entries.proposition: Primary result: no difference in Bayley-III cognitive or Vineland-II composites at 12 or 24 months.
entries.snippet: No differences were found between participants randomized to vigabatrin or placebo with respect to Bayley-III cognitive composite or Vineland-II adaptive behavior composite standard scores at 12, 24 months of age.

entries.proposition: Drug-resistant epilepsy at 24 months was 48 versus 52 percent, against 28 versus 64 percent in the earlier open-label trial.
entries.snippet: We found no difference in drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) at 24 months of age (48% in TSC infants randomized to early vigabatrin vs. 52% in TSC infants randomized to placebo)

entries.proposition: The earlier trial had reported a reduction in drug resistance of 28 versus 64 percent.
entries.snippet: In contrast, EPISTOP reported a reduction in DRE in the early vigabatrin group (28%) vs. conventional treatment (64%)

entries.proposition: Infantile spasms were later and less frequent on the drug (hazard ratio 0.263), but the comparison was not specified in advance and was not tested.
entries.snippet: These comparisons, however, were not specified a priori, and thus no statistical hypothesis testing was performed.

entries.proposition: The authors state the developmental rationale rested on the effect on spasms, with minimal rationale that GABA would be pro-cognitive.
entries.snippet: with minimal rationale that increased GABA would be pro-cognitive, the proposed improvement in neurocognition was based on the efficacy of vigabatrin in preventing infantile spasms in TSC

entries.proposition: Delaying or preventing spasms had no measurable effect on cognition at two years.
entries.snippet: our data demonstrates that delay or prevention of infantile spasms had no measurable effect on cognitive outcomes at two years of life.

entries.proposition: The authors suggest exposure rather than timing may matter because the placebo arm soon received the drug.
entries.snippet: Perhaps timing of vigabatrin treatment initiation is less important than overall exposure to vigabatrin at these early ages in TSC infants.

entries.proposition: Genotype was unevenly distributed: milder TSC1 and no-mutation cases enriched in the placebo arm.
entries.snippet: TSC1 mutations and NMI/VUS were enriched in the placebo group vs. the vigabatrin treatment group.

entries.proposition: Infants randomised before 7 months had lower cognitive scores irrespective of arm.
entries.snippet: However, those randomized before 7 months’ age had lower cognitive measures irrespective of treatment group.

entries.proposition: The authors note that norm-referenced standard scores may mask within-person changes.
entries.snippet: We used norm-referenced standard scores as the primary outcome for assessing development, but these may mask changes in skills within and across individuals.

entries.proposition: The EEG biomarker had a positive predictive value of 0.73 and a negative predictive value of 0.73.
entries.snippet: Thus, the positive predictive value of the EEG biomarker was 0.731(19/19+7=19/26), and a negative predictive value was 0.733 (11/11+4=11/15).

entries.proposition: Table 3: Bayley-III cognitive composite at 24 months 80.9 on drug and 83.9 on placebo.
entries.anchor: Table 3, Bayley-III cognitive composite 24 month row

entries.proposition: Table 2 refractory percentages do not match their counts (9 of 29 printed as 28 percent; 12 of 27 as 22 percent).
Conclusion: EEG-triggered preventive treatment did not improve cognition or adaptive behaviour at 24 months.
entries.snippet: preventative treatment with vigabatrin based on EEG epileptiform activity did not improve cognition (measured by the Bayley-III) or adaptive behaviors (measured by the Vineland-II) at 24 months of age.
